body:
Sanchi: A monument built over several periods

Sanchi is an important Buddhist archaeological site in Madhya Pradesh, near Vidisha and Bhopal. The Great Stupa, usually called Stupa 1, is particularly important because its surviving architecture records several stages of construction and enlargement.

The earliest brick core of the Great Stupa is associated with Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE. The monument did not acquire all its present features during Ashoka's lifetime. Its expansion and elaborate sculptural decoration developed over subsequent centuries.

Major stages in the development of the Great Stupa

  • Mauryan period, 3rd century BCE: The original brick stupa was established under Ashokan patronage.
  • Shunga period, especially 2nd century BCE: The stupa was enlarged, faced with stone and provided with additional architectural features, including railings and stairways.
  • Later post-Mauryan period, especially 1st century BCE: Elaborately carved gateways were added under Satavahana-period patronage.

This sequence explains why the Great Stupa is associated with Ashoka even though much of the sculpture visible today is later. A monument's foundation date and the date of its surviving decorative elements need not be identical.

Distinctive features of Sanchi Stupa 1

The Great Stupa has a large hemispherical mound surrounded by a stone railing. Its developed form includes 4 ornamental gateways positioned in the principal directions. It also has an upper circumambulatory path, in addition to the lower path around the mound.

The gateways, known as toranas, have upright pillars supporting sculptured horizontal members. Their surfaces depict episodes from the Buddha's life, Jataka stories, animals, trees and auspicious figures.

Among the recurring images is the shalabhanjika, a female figure associated with a tree. Such figures show how established regional and popular artistic symbols were incorporated into Buddhist architectural decoration.

The carvings also use symbolic representations of the Buddha, such as an empty throne or a wheel. This is characteristic of an early phase in Buddhist narrative art, before large human images of the Buddha became common.

Other stupas at Sanchi

Sanchi is not a single-stupa site. It contains several stupas and other monuments. Stupa 3 is associated with the relics of Sariputta and Mahamoggallana, important disciples of the Buddha. The entire complex also contains later shrines and temples, including remains from the Gupta period.

One site, several historical periods

The Mauryan origin of Sanchi Stupa 1 does not make every gateway, sculpture or temple at Sanchi a Mauryan creation. Identify the construction phase of the particular feature being described.

Gujarat connection: Ashoka's Girnar rock edicts

At Girnar near Junagadh, Gujarat, Ashoka caused inscriptions to be engraved on a large rock. These are commonly identified as the 14 Major Rock Edicts and are generally dated to around 250 BCE.

The Girnar inscriptions are important evidence of the spread of Ashoka's messages to western India. They demonstrate the use of a natural rock surface as a medium of royal communication.

The same rock also preserves inscriptions from later periods, including those associated with Rudradaman and the Gupta ruler Skandagupta. The inscriptions therefore document different historical periods at a single location. They should not be treated as if they were all issued by Ashoka.

Gujarat connection: the Buddhist stupa at Devni Mori

Devni Mori, near Shamlaji in Aravalli district, is an important Buddhist archaeological site in Gujarat. Excavations revealed the remains of a substantial brick stupa, associated monastic structures and a relic casket. The site demonstrates that Buddhist religious architecture developed in Gujarat beyond the Mauryan heartland.

The important distinction is chronological. The principal Buddhist establishment at Devni Mori belongs to the early centuries CE, especially around the 4th century CE, and continued into later centuries. It is associated with the Western Kshatrapa-period cultural setting, rather than being identified as one of Ashoka's original 3rd-century BCE stupas.

Consequently, Girnar and Devni Mori represent different kinds of archaeological evidence. Girnar preserves Ashokan rock inscriptions; Devni Mori preserves the remains of a later Buddhist stupa and monastic complex.

Prelims focus

  • Sanchi Great Stupa, or Stupa 1, is located in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Its original brick core is associated with Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE.
  • Major enlargement took place in the Shunga period; richly carved gateways belong to a later phase.
  • Sanchi Stupa 1 has 4 gateways and an upper circumambulatory path.
  • Girnar near Junagadh preserves Ashoka's 14 Major Rock Edicts.
  • Trap: Devni Mori in Gujarat is a later Buddhist stupa site, not the location of the Sarnath Lion Capital or an original Ashokan pillar.

[Sources: Archaeological Survey of India, Buddhist Monuments at Sanchi, sections on Mauryan, Shunga, Satavahana and Gupta phases, consulted 23 November 2026; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4, Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, printed pp. 46–47; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 96–102; Government of Gujarat, Junagadh District, Ashok Shilalekh, consulted 23 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Arvalli District, Devni Mori, consulted 23 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Buddhist Monuments, section on Devnimori, consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The important stages of Sanchi's development extend beyond the Mauryan period.

title: Sanchi Stupa and the Mauryan Buddhist Heritage of Gujarat

body:
Temple building during the Gupta period

The Gupta period, broadly from the 4th to the 6th century CE, was an important stage in the development of Indian temple architecture. Builders increasingly constructed permanent, free-standing shrines in stone and brick. Some surviving temples are simple structures, while others show the beginnings of the elevated temple tower associated with later North Indian architecture.

The most important development was the gradual establishment of a recognisable temple plan centred on a room containing the principal religious image. This form was subsequently elaborated through porches, platforms, sculptured doorways and towers.

It would be incorrect to assume that temples or image worship began only with the Guptas. Earlier religious shrines existed, including structures built from less durable materials. The significance of Gupta architecture is that it provides particularly important surviving examples of the early structural temple.

Basic parts of an early Gupta temple

  • Garbhagriha: The central sanctum containing the principal image or object of worship. In many early temples, it was a small, square room with a single entrance.
  • Mandapa: A hall or porch situated before the sanctum. Early examples often have a shallow porch supported by pillars.
  • Plinth: The supporting platform on which the temple stands. Some later Gupta examples have a more prominent raised platform.
  • Shikhara: The tower rising above the sanctum. This element became increasingly important in developed North Indian temples, but early surviving Gupta shrines did not all possess a tall tower.
  • Decorated doorway: The entrance often became an important place for sculpture, including representations of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna.

In a typical early arrangement, worshippers approached the temple through the porch and faced the main image inside the garbhagriha. As the architectural form developed, the tower above the sanctum emphasised the sacred centre of the building.

Structural and rock-cut architecture

A structural temple is assembled from building materials such as stone blocks or bricks. A rock-cut shrine is created by removing rock from an existing hill or rock mass. Both forms existed in ancient India, but they are constructed differently.

Sanchi Temple 17: The simple early Gupta type

Temple 17 at Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh, dates to the early 5th century CE and is an important surviving example of a Gupta-period structural temple.

It has a modest square sanctum, a flat roof and a porch supported by 4 pillars. Its appearance is comparatively restrained, with little elaborate sculpture on the main walls.

This temple demonstrates that a fully developed, towering shikhara was not an essential feature of the earliest surviving Gupta structures. The clear arrangement of sanctum and porch is more important for understanding its architectural stage.

Other important early Gupta examples

Tigawa, Madhya Pradesh

The Kankali Devi Temple at Tigawa is another example of an early Gupta stone temple. It is associated with the simple arrangement of a small sanctum and a pillared entrance porch.

Udayagiri, near Vidisha, Madhya Pradesh

The Udayagiri complex contains important Gupta-period rock-cut shrines and associated architectural remains. Its significance lies partly in showing that rock-cut sanctuaries and structural construction existed alongside one another during the period.

Bhitargaon, Uttar Pradesh

The Bhitargaon Temple is an important example of early brick temple architecture. Unlike the simple flat-roofed type represented by Sanchi Temple 17, it is associated with a prominent rising superstructure. It shows how brick as well as stone could be used to construct substantial religious buildings.

Development towards the Nagara temple form

In North India, a major later development was the Nagara temple style, especially associated with the tower rising above the sanctum. An early form of this tower is the latina or rekha-prasada shikhara, whose outline rises upward and curves inward towards the top.

Gupta temples help explain the transition from a simple square shrine with a porch to a more elaborate structure with a raised platform and a shikhara. The development was gradual, and different forms coexisted rather than replacing one another everywhere at the same time.

Prelims focus

  • The Gupta period broadly covers the 4th–6th centuries CE.
  • Garbhagriha is the sanctum; mandapa is the hall or porch.
  • Sanchi Temple 17 is an early 5th-century Gupta structural temple in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Temple 17 has a flat roof and a porch supported by 4 pillars.
  • Bhitargaon in Uttar Pradesh is an important Gupta-period brick temple.
  • Trap: Not all Gupta temples had tall shikharas; the earliest surviving structural examples could be flat-roofed.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 69–72; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 12, Buildings, Paintings and Books, printed pp. 123–124, 2018–19 reprint; Archaeological Survey of India and UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Serial Nomination of Gupta Temples in North India, entry on Temple 17 at Sanchi, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Gupta Temples: Early Structural Architecture and the Emergence of the Shikhara

body:
Location and historical importance

The Vishnu Temple at Deogarh, commonly called the Dashavatara Temple, is located near Lalitpur in Uttar Pradesh. It belongs to the late Gupta architectural tradition and is generally dated to the early 6th century CE.

The temple is especially important because it brings together a raised platform, a planned arrangement of subsidiary shrines, sculptured walls and an early form of the North Indian shikhara. These features make it more architecturally developed than a simple flat-roofed shrine such as Sanchi Temple 17.

The original temple is not completely preserved. Its surviving portions nevertheless provide important evidence for the emergence of the early Nagara temple form.

The meaning of the Panchayatana plan

The Deogarh temple is associated with the Panchayatana arrangement. In this architectural plan, a principal shrine occupies the centre of a platform, while 4 smaller subsidiary shrines are placed at the corners.

The total number of shrines in the complete arrangement is therefore 5: one central shrine and four corner shrines.

The term Panchayatana describes the arrangement of the shrines. It does not mean that every one of the five shrines must be dedicated to a different deity, or that their original dedications can always be established.

Early Nagara features

The central sanctum of the Deogarh temple stands on a raised platform. The temple also preserves evidence of an early curvilinear shikhara, associated with the latina or rekha-prasada form of North Indian temple architecture.

The shikhara rises above the garbhagriha, placing architectural emphasis on the chamber containing the principal image. This relationship between sanctum and tower became a characteristic feature of later Nagara temples.

The Deogarh temple is therefore valuable not because it possesses all the elaborate features of much later North Indian temples, but because it shows an important stage in the development of their basic architectural form.

The 3 major Vishnu relief panels

The Deogarh temple is also celebrated for sculptural panels depicting different forms or episodes associated with Vishnu. The placement of the major panels is useful for identifying the monument.

  • South wall — Sheshashayana or Anantashayana: Vishnu is shown reclining on the serpent Ananta or Shesha.
  • East wall — Nara-Narayana: The panel depicts the figures of Nara and Narayana.
  • North wall — Gajendramoksha: The panel represents the story of Vishnu's rescue of Gajendra, the elephant devotee.

These panels demonstrate the growing importance of narrative religious sculpture on temple walls. They also help distinguish a Gupta-period Vishnu temple from a Buddhist stupa, whose primary form and religious purpose are different.

The entrance doorway

The temple faces west, an important detail because many Indian temples face east. Its entrance is decorated with figures of the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna.

Such river-goddess imagery became an important feature of North Indian temple entrances. The figures were associated with auspiciousness and the symbolic purification of the person entering the sacred space.

Why the name Dashavatara requires care

The temple is widely known as the Dashavatara Temple because of its association with Vishnu. However, the original deities of the 4 subsidiary shrines are not securely known.

It is therefore incorrect to assume, merely from the modern name, that each subsidiary shrine definitely contained a particular avatar of Vishnu. The secure architectural point is the Panchayatana arrangement of 5 shrines; the exact original dedications of the corner shrines remain uncertain.

Identify Deogarh through 3 clues

Deogarh is a late Gupta Vishnu temple in Uttar Pradesh, associated with the Panchayatana arrangement, an early Nagara shikhara and 3 major Vishnu relief panels.

Prelims focus

  • The Deogarh Vishnu Temple is located near Lalitpur, Uttar Pradesh.
  • It is generally dated to the early 6th century CE.
  • Panchayatana means 1 principal shrine with 4 subsidiary shrines, making 5 in all.
  • The temple represents an early stage of Nagara architecture with a curvilinear shikhara.
  • Its major panels are Sheshashayana on the south, Nara-Narayana on the east and Gajendramoksha on the north.
  • Trap: The name Dashavatara does not establish the original dedication of every subsidiary shrine.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 72–73; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 104–106.]

pictures.caption: Deogarh preserves an important stage in the development of Gupta-period stone temples.
